analysis.one_liner: Guarantees part-time workers family leave eligibility, equal pay for equal work, and first chance at extra hours.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in December 2025 with 34 cosponsors, all Democrats, and has been referred to four House committees with no hearing, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite two sets of rules that today treat part-time and temporary workers differently from full-timers. First, it would make anyone who has worked 90 days eligible for unpaid, job-protected family and medical leave, replacing the current requirement of a year on the job and 1,250 hours worked, which screens out most part-timers. Second, it would bar employers from paying part-timers less, giving them fewer benefits, or holding back promotions for jobs requiring substantially equal work, and would require employers to offer available hours to existing employees who have asked for them before hiring anyone new through an outside agency or contractor.
analysis.who_benefits: Part-time and temporary workers — retail clerks, food-service workers, caregivers, and others working fewer than 35 hours a week — who today can be paid less than full-time coworkers doing the same work, are excluded from family and medical leave, and watch new hires or agency temps get the hours they wanted.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the family and medical leave eligibility requirement of 12 months on the job and 1,250 hours in the past year with a 90-day employment requirement, opening job-protected leave to most part-time workers; the same change applies to congressional staff and federal employees.

Bars employers from paying part-timers less, giving them less input into their schedules, prorating them out of benefits and time off, or denying them promotions, when their jobs require substantially equal skill, effort, and responsibility under similar conditions.

Requires employers to record each new hire's desired weekly hours and availability, and to offer available hours to existing employees who want them before hiring from outside — including through temp agencies or contractors — and to pay existing employees for hours they asked for that went instead to a new hire.

Gives workers remedies including back pay, lost benefits, interest, and doubled (liquidated) damages in court, plus Labor Department investigations and civil penalties of $1,100 to $5,000 per retaliatory act, and prohibits firing or cutting hours in retaliation.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely heavily on part-time and temporary labor — retail chains, restaurants and hotels, franchised businesses, and staffing agencies — would bear higher benefit costs, scheduling and recordkeeping requirements, and exposure to lawsuits and penalties.

drawbacks.text: The equal-treatment rule requires employers to provide part-timers pro rata paid time off and other benefits, and the hours-offer rule requires scheduling systems, written availability statements, and three years of records; for businesses with high turnover and volatile demand this is a real cost that would likely be passed to consumers or absorbed in fewer openings.

Under the bill, an employer generally cannot bring in a temp or contractor to cover hours an existing employee has said they want to work, which limits a flexibility tool many businesses use to cover sudden absences and demand spikes.
The bill counts employees across an entire franchise network or integrated enterprise, so franchise operators who individually employ few people can be covered by the new rules.
Extending family and medical leave eligibility to employees after only 90 days means employers may face longer absences from newer workers with less tenure to plan around.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the bill addresses a real gap: roughly the same job can pay differently depending on how many hours it is scheduled for, and the 1,250-hour leave rule excludes exactly the people most likely to lack paid sick leave or savings. The costs fall on employers, not workers, and are real but ordinary labor-law compliance costs; the hours-offer and pay-for-unfilled-hours provisions are the most administratively demanding parts and the ones businesses would contest hardest. The bill is plainly weighted toward workers, with exceptions built in for qualifications, overtime thresholds, and unreachable employees.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on December 17, 2025 and sent to four House committees; none of them has taken it up, and no vote has happened yet.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the Part-Time Worker Bill of Rights Act in the House on December 17, 2025, with 32 additional original cosponsors.

It was referred to the Committees on Education and Workforce, House Administration, Oversight and Government Reform, and Judiciary; splitting a bill across multiple committees gives each chair independent power to stall it.
The bill has 34 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no Republican support in the record.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote has occurred since referral, and the Congress runs through January 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers of part-time and temporary workers, who keep the current two-tier pay and leave rules as long as the bill sits without action.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers of part-time workers, for now

sides.party_line_note: All 34 cosponsors are Democrats, there are no Republican cosponsors, and with Republicans holding the House majority no committee action or vote has occurred.

industries.note: These industries run on part-time schedules and would have to prorate benefits, equalize pay for substantially equal work, and offer existing employees hours before hiring outsiders. The bill's costs land directly on this labor model.
Employers could no longer use staffing agencies or contractors to fill hours that existing employees have asked to work, cutting into the placement volume the industry sells.
The bill counts employees across a franchisor's whole network, so franchise systems with more than 15 workers in aggregate are covered even where a single franchisee employs few people.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no committee action two months after referral, and the bill split across four committees, the most likely path is that it never receives a hearing or vote and dies when this Congress ends in January 2027, the fate of most partisan labor bills in a divided House.
